notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 43, drawn from the sources found.

## General Background

Psalm 43 is the only psalm in Book 2 (Psalms 42–72) that has no heading. Many scholars note that in some ancient Hebrew manuscripts, Psalms 42 and 43 are joined as one. G. Campbell Morgan says it “is either a part of the previous one or is closely connected with it.” Spurgeon believed the style of poetry pleased the writer, who later “wrote this supplemental hymn after the same manner. As an appendix it needed no title.” Both psalms share the repeated refrain (42:5, 11; 43:5) and the theme of spiritual depression leading to hope. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/psalms-43.html; spurgeon.org archive excerpt)

---

## v. 1 — “Vindicate me, O God, and plead my case against an ungodly nation; deliver me from deceitful and unjust men.”

**Traditional Reading**

The psalmist cries out for God to act as judge and advocate. David Guzik notes that the psalmist “felt unjustly accused and took his sense of injustice to the right place – to the throne of God, and he left his vindication up to God.” This is a recurring theme in the Psalms (cf. Psalm 35:24; 26:1; 7:9). (enduringword.com)

Spurgeon writes: “Others are unable to understand my motives, and unwilling to give me a just verdict. My heart is clear as to intent and therefore I bring my case before thee… If thou wilt judge, thy acceptance of my conduct will be enough for me; I can laugh at human misrepresentation.” (spurgeon.org, search excerpt)

**Who are the enemies?** Gill suggests the “ungodly nation” could be the Philistines, or David’s own nation who joined Absalom’s rebellion. The “deceitful and unjust man” may be Absalom (who used a pretended vow to deceive David), Ahithophel (David’s former friend turned traitor), or Saul (who pursued David under pretence of friendship). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/43.htm) The Pulpit Commentary likewise identifies either Absalom or Ahithophel, while noting “man” could be used abstractly for David’s enemies generally. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/43.htm)

Ellicott notes that “ungodly nation” in Hebrew is simply a negative term — *a nation not khasîd*, i.e., not in the covenant — but naturally a positive sense of ungodliness attaches to it. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/43.htm)

Clarke sees the psalmist speaking “in the person of the whole Israelitish people then captive in Babylon.” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-43.html)

---

## v. 2 — “For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression?”

**Traditional Reading**

The psalmist simultaneously affirms his trust and voices his perplexity. Guzik: “If the psalmist didn’t have a relationship with God, he wouldn’t have this problem. Yet he did love the Lord, and his trust was in the strength of God and not his own strength – so he wondered where God was at his critical moment of need.” The repeated “Why?” is “familiar to the tested people of faith.” (enduringword.com)

Spurgeon calls the “For” an “argument, which is the very sinew of prayer. If we reasoned more with the Lord we should have more victories in supplication.” He notes the threefold confession: “All my strength belongs to thee… All my strength comes from thee… All my strength is in thee, I leave therefore this task of combating my foes entirely in thy hands.” Regarding “Why dost thou cast me off?” Spurgeon says, “There are many reasons why the Lord might cast us off, but no reason shall prevail to make him do so. He hath not cast off his people, though he for awhile treats them as cast offs.” (spurgeon.org, search excerpt)

Gill adds that the language of being “cast off” is “the language of unbelief: it being what was not in reality, only in appearance.” God never truly casts off His people; they “always continue in his love, and in his covenant, and in the hands of his Son.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/43.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that “Why dost thou cast me off?” is equivalent to the “Why hast thou forgotten me?” of Psalm 42:9. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/43.htm)

---

## v. 3 — “Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain, and to the place where You dwell.”

**Traditional Reading**

This is the turning point of the psalm. Guzik calls it the beginning of the “procession of praise.” He notes the psalmist “knew that his light and his truth were not enough – he needed the light and truth of God. It wasn’t within him, so if God didn’t send it, he would not have it.” The prayer “Let them lead me” is “a prayer of submission.” Guzik quotes Spurgeon: “We seek not light to sin by, nor truth to be exalted by it, but that they may become our practical guides to the nearest communion with God.” (enduringword.com)

**What are “light” and “truth”?**

- **Poole** (via Guzik): “Thy favour, or the light of thy countenance, and the truth of thy promises made to me.” (enduringword.com)
- **Gill**: “By light is meant… the light of God’s countenance, the discoveries of his favour and lovingkindness, which produce light, life, joy, peace, and comfort.” Some Jewish interpreters understood it as the Messiah, the Sun of Righteousness. By “truth” Gill understands “the faithfulness of God in the fulfilment of his promises.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/43.htm)
- **Ellicott**: Instead of the violent escort of Assyrian soldiers leading the exile away from the holy hill, “the poet prays for God’s light and truth to lead him, like two angel guides, back to it.” He calls them “the Urim and Thummim of the saints (Deuteronomy 33:8), the promised attendants of Israel… the escort of all faithful souls in all ages.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/43.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Both words “equally signify God’s favour.” As the pillar of fire and cloud led Israel, so let God’s light and truth lead David back to Jerusalem and the holy hill of Zion. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/43.htm)
- **Constable**: “God’s light is the revelation of His will that brings understanding and life. His truth rests in His Word that reveals that will.” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-43.html)

**“Your holy mountain… Your dwelling-place”**: This refers to Mount Zion and the tabernacle. In his exile, “it was David’s most earnest desire to revisit the tabernacle which he had set up on Mount Zion, where God’s presence dwelt.” He had made his return to it a test of God’s favour (2 Samuel 15:25-26). (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/43.htm) Gill notes the tabernacle is called “tabernacles” (plural) because of the holy place and the most holy place (cf. Hebrews 9:2), representing “the church and ordinances of God.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/43.htm)

---

## v. 4 — “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God.”

**Traditional Reading**

This is the destination of the “procession of praise.” Morgan (via Guzik) traces three stops: the tabernacle (God’s presence), the altar, and then praise itself. “The way to God is ever the way of the altar. The way to the altar is opened by the sending out of light and truth from God.” (enduringword.com)

**The altar**: Guzik notes this would not be a sacrifice of atonement for sin, “but for gratitude and celebration of fellowship with God.” Under the New Covenant, this points to the cross of Christ — Hebrews 13:10. “When we follow the light and truth of the LORD, it will lead us to His altar – the cross where Jesus was given as a sacrifice for our sins.” (enduringword.com) Gill likewise identifies the altar under the Gospel dispensation as Christ (Hebrews 13:10). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/43.htm)

**“God my exceeding joy”**: The Hebrew is literally “God, the gladness of my exultation” (Pulpit). Spurgeon writes: “He is not his joy alone, but his exceeding joy; not the fountain of joy, the giver of joy, or the maintainer of joy, but that joy itself. The margin hath it, ‘The gladness of my joy,’ i.e., the soul, the essence, the very bowels of my joy.” (spurgeon.org, search excerpt)

**Protestant Distinctive – Reformed Baptist (Piper / “Christian Hedonism”)**: John Piper preached on Psalm 43 multiple times, calling Psalm 43:4 the “ultimate goal of life.” He interprets “God my exceeding joy” as meaning that God is not merely the giver of joy but is Himself the joy: “The final goal of life is not forgiveness or any of God’s good gifts. The final goal of life is God himself, experienced as your exceeding joy.” Piper translates literally: “God, the gladness of my rejoicing.” He says, “Every joy that does not have God as the central gladness of the joy is a hollow joy and in the end will burst like a bubble.” Piper also notes that “authentic joy in God will overflow with praises” — praise “not merely expresses but completes the enjoyment; it is its appointed consummation” (citing C.S. Lewis). (desiringgod.org, search excerpts)

**The harp**: Gill notes the harp was “typical of that spiritual melody made in the hearts of God’s people when they sing his praise” (Revelation 5:8). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/43.htm)

---

## v. 5 — “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.”

**Traditional Reading**

This is the identical refrain from Psalm 42:5 and 42:11. Guzik observes that “at the end of the psalm, none of the circumstances of the psalmist had changed – only his attitude, and what a difference that made.” The psalmist “would not surrender to his feelings of depression and discouragement. Instead, he challenged those feelings and brought them to God.” (enduringword.com)

Morgan: “Not yet has the answer come. The darkness and the mystery are still about him, but the shining way is seen; and again the soul is forbidden to despair and hope is encouraged in God.” (enduringword.com, citing Morgan)

Spurgeon: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? If God be thine, why this dejection? If he uplifts thee, why art thou so near the ground? The dew of love is falling, O withering heart, revive.” He adds: “Hope in God, or wait for God. There is need of patience, but there is ground for hope.” (spurgeon.org, search excerpt)

**“The help of my countenance”**: Guzik notes the Hebrew word carries the sense of salvation more than help: “God saves the countenance of His people.” Kidner is quoted: “The poet can praise God as his ‘exceeding joy’ and – not merely his help, which is too weak a word – his ‘salvation.’ Outwardly nothing has changed: but he has won through.” Boice adds: “Is there a cure for depression? Yes. But it is not in us. It is in God. The cure is to seek God’s face, so ours will not be downcast, which is what the psalmist does.” Maclaren: “Faith may have a long struggle with fear, but it will have the last word, and that word will be ‘the help of my countenance and my God.’” (enduringword.com)

**Piper’s emphasis — preaching to yourself**: Piper identifies two spiritual strategies in this psalm. The first (vv. 3–4) is speaking to God in prayer — “Send out your light.” The second (v. 5) is speaking to your own soul: “Why are you cast down, O my soul? … Hope in God.” Piper says, “Learn to preach to yourself. Preach the gospel to yourself.” He calls these “the two great practical steps you can take when you feel forsaken: pray to God and preach to yourself. Nothing is more important in your mind than preaching the gospel to yourself. Preaching hope when all your circumstances are preaching despair.” (desiringgod.org, search excerpts)

---

## Denominational Perspectives

The distinctively different readings across traditions are modest for this psalm. Most commentators agree on its basic meaning.

**Baptist (Spurgeon)**: Emphasises personal faith, the individual’s direct access to God, and the duty of the believer to challenge his own despondency. Spurgeon sees the altar in v. 4 as foreshadowing Christ, but the emphasis remains on the believer’s heart-attitude of joy in God, not ritual. (spurgeon.org)

**Reformed Baptist / “Christian Hedonism” (Piper)**: Distinctively stresses v. 4 as teaching that God Himself is our supreme joy — not just His gifts. This is the hallmark of Piper’s “Christian Hedonism”: “God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in Him.” (desiringgod.org)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)**: Guzik (whose commentary is widely used in charismatic and evangelical circles) reads the “procession of praise” as a spiritual journey applicable to believers experiencing depression. He emphasises that the Holy Spirit’s light and truth lead believers today, and that worship and the cross are the remedy for a downcast spirit. (enduringword.com)

**Reformed (G. Campbell Morgan)**: Stresses the structured “procession” — to the hill, to the tabernacles, to the altar, then praise — as a pattern of approaching God that remains valid. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/psalms-43.html)

**Lutheran and Methodist**: No distinct Lutheran or Methodist commentaries on this specific psalm were found in the search results from lcms.org, 1517.org, wesley.nnu.edu, or seedbed.com.

**Catholic and Orthodox**: No results were found from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits.

**Modern Scholarship**: No specific results were found from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the search limits.

## Summary

Psalm 43 traces a journey from distress to praise in five movements: (1) a cry for vindication against deceitful enemies, (2) an honest lament asking “why” God seems distant, (3) a pivotal prayer for God’s light and truth to lead the way home to worship, (4) an anticipatory vow to come to God’s altar with exuberant joy and harp-song, and (5) a self-exhortation to hope in God despite unchanged circumstances. The psalm is universally read as a model for dealing with spiritual depression: take your complaint to God, ask for His guiding light, set your sights on His presence and the cross, and preach hope to your own soul.
